{{short description|American physicist and kinetic sculptor}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2012}}
'''John Rosenbaum''' (September 3, 1934<ref>"Cornell Elects Rosenbaum", New York Times, Dec 4, 1954
"John J Rosenbaum Jr of Brigantine N J today was elected captain of Cornell's 1955 varsity crosscountry team"</ref> – September 30, 2003) was an American [[physicist]], educator<ref>{{cite web |url=http://arts.endow.gov/about/AnnualReports/NEA-Annual-Report-1982.pdf |title=National Endowment for the Arts Annual Report 1982 |access-date=January 17, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111016154555/http://arts.endow.gov/about/AnnualReports/NEA-Annual-Report-1982.pdf |archive-date=October 16, 2011 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> and [[Kinetic art|kinetic sculptor]],<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.jweekly.com/article/full/6286/parkinson-s-fails-to-squelch-artistry-of-a-former-scientist/ |title=August 8, 1997 "Parkinson's fails to squelch artistry of a former scientist", Ronnie Caplane, ''Jewish Bulletin'', August 8, 1997 |newspaper=J |publisher=Jweekly.com |date=August 8, 1997 |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref> associated with the [[San Francisco Renaissance]]<ref>''[[Art in the San Francisco Bay Area (book)|Art in the San Francisco Bay Area, 1945–1980]]'', Thomas Albright. University Presses of [[University of California Press|California]], [[Columbia University Press|Columbia]] and [[Princeton University Press|Princeton]], 1985, {{ISBN|0-520-05518-7}} (p. 172)</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aGN3vXcZl74C&q=%22john+rosenbaum%22+%22light+boxes%22&pg=PA172|title=Art in the San Francisco Bay Area, 1945-1980: An Illustrated History|isbn=9780520051935|last1=Albright|first1=Thomas|date=January 1985|publisher=University of California Press }}</ref> and the [[counterculture of the 1960s]].

==Early life and education==
Rosenbaum was born on September 3, 1934, in [[Brigantine, New Jersey]]. He attended [[Cornell University]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cornellbigred.com/sports/2009/7/20/MXC_0720091558.aspx?path=mcross |title=Cornell University Men's Cross Country History webpage |publisher=Cornellbigred.com |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=[ Displaying Abstract ] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1954/12/04/archives/cornell-elects-rosenbaum.html |title="Cornell Elects Rosenbaum", New York Times, Dec. 4, 1954 |publisher=Select.nytimes.com |date=December 4, 1954 |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref> where he graduated with a degree in [[engineering physics]] in 1957.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://hepstrack.com/championships/heps-cross-country/mens-results/the-1950s/1953-2/ |title=Archived copy |access-date=May 24, 2012 |archive-date=October 12, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111012104943/http://hepstrack.com/championships/heps-cross-country/mens-results/the-1950s/1953-2/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:TCMI Creative Playthings Xylopipes 3.jpg|thumb|Xylopipes, designed by Rosenbaum for [[Creative Playthings]], {{Circa|1960s}}]]
After graduated from Cornell University in 1957, Rosenbaum moved to the [[San Francisco Bay Area]] in the early 1960s, where he contributed to the [[Harvard Project Physics]] textbooks.<ref>''Project Physics: Text'' Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1975 edition, {{ISBN|0-03-089634-7}}, appendix p. A23</ref> He was associated with the [[free school movement]] in the 1960s, and was a colleague of the educator [[Herbert Kohl (educator)|Herbert Kohl]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://negroartist.com/writings/BLACK%20PANTHER%20NEWSPAPERS/9%20no%2030.htm |title="Black Panther Newspaper", "Center for Open Learning and Teaching" workshop notice, ca. 1973 |publisher=Negroartist.com |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref> who described Rosenbaum's educational work in his book ''The Open Classroom''<ref>''The Open Classroom: A Practical Guide to a New Way of Teaching'', Herbert R. Kohl. New York Review/Vintage Books, 1969, pp. 64–65</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vidyaonline.org/dl/openclassroom.pdf |title=''The Open Classroom'' online text, p. 24 |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref> and ''Math, Writing & Games in the Open Classroom''.<ref>''Math, Writing and Games in the Open Classroom'', Herbert R. Kohl. New York Review/Vintage Books, 1974, {{ISBN|0-394-70995-0}}, pp. 134–136</ref> He designed the Xylopipes [[xylophone]] children's toy for [[Creative Playthings]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.jweekly.com/article/full/6286/parkinson-s-fails-to-squelch-artistry-of-a-former-scientist/|title = Parkinsons fails to squelch artistry of a former scientist| newspaper=J |date = August 8, 1997}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/theithacajournal/obituary.aspx?n=john-jacob-rosenbaum&pid=87919205|title = John Jacob Rosenbaum Jr. Obituary (2003) Ithaca Journal|website = [[Legacy.com]]}}</ref>

Rosenbaum created "Light Boxes",<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ecatalogue.art.yale.edu/detail.htm?objectId=89923 |title="Untitled Kinetic Construction", 1968. Yale University Art Gallery |publisher=Ecatalogue.art.yale.edu |access-date=January 17, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306003601/http://ecatalogue.art.yale.edu/detail.htm?objectId=89923 |archive-date=March 6, 2012 |df=mdy-all }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/89923 | title=Untitled Kinetic Construction &#124; Yale University Art Gallery }}</ref> [[Lumino Kinetic Art|kinetic sculptures]] using [[Polaroid (polarizer)|polarized]] light and layers of [[cellophane]] laminated between pairs of rotating glass disks, producing changing patterns and [[Polarization (waves)#Materials science|colors]] similar to, and on a smaller scale than, [[Liquid light shows|light shows]] projected at rock concerts in the 1960s. He was exhibited by the [[Felix Landau (art)|Landau Gallery]]<ref name="worldcat1969">{{cite web|url=http://www.worldcat.org/wcpa/ow/22156732 |title=John Rosenbaum: kinetic constructions with polarized light: exhibition May 26 – June 21, 1969, Felix Landau Gallery |publisher=Worldcat.org |date=June 21, 1969 |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref> in [[La Cienega Boulevard|Beverly Hills]], among others.<ref>Andrews, Oliver. ''Electric Art'', exhibition catalog. Los Angeles: UCLA Art Department, 1969</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-05-23-ca-2090-story.html | work=Los Angeles Times | first=Leah | last=Ollman | title=ART REVIEW : Walbridge Exhibit's Power Weakened by Indulgence | date=May 23, 1988}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://archives.newyorker.com/default.aspx?iid=16463&startpage=page0000012 |title=''The New Yorker'', Jan. 6, 1968, digital edition |publisher=Archives.newyorker.com |access-date=January 17, 2012}}</ref><ref>"John Rosenbaum: Constructions with polarized light by a physicist-artist;", ''The New Yorker'' Jan. 6, 1968, p. 10, E. 84th St. gallery listing</ref> He was a colleague of silk screen artist [[Arthur Okamura]]. He designed the original logo for [[Herbie Mann]]'s [[Embryo Records]].

==Exhibitions==
*1969 [[Felix Landau (art)|Felix Landau Gallery]], Los Angeles<ref name="worldcat1969"/>
*1975 [[Walnut Creek, California]] (with Arthur Okamura)<ref>Thompson, Peter, ed.; "John Rosenbaum and Arthur Okamura", Catalogue, The Civic Arts Gallery, May 21 – June 28, 1975</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bquayartgallery.com/artists/okamura_bio.html |title=Arthur Okamura Exhibitions/Bibliography, Braunstein/Quay Gallery website |publisher=Bquayartgallery.com |access-date=January 17, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224134134/http://www.bquayartgallery.com/artists/okamura_bio.html |archive-date=February 24, 2012 }}</ref>

==Death==
Rosenbaum died in [[Alameda, California]], on September 30, 2003, from complications of [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref>[http://cornellalumnimagazine.com/Archive/2004julaug/notes/obits.html "Cornell Alumni Magazine" July/Aug. 2004 V. 107 # 1, Alumni Deaths] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060516015259/http://cornellalumnimagazine.com/Archive/2004julaug/notes/obits.html |date=May 16, 2006 }}</ref>
